original_value: Simulator training for image-guided surgical interventions would benefit from intelligent systems that detect the evolution of task performance, and take control of individual speed–precision strategies by providing effective automatic performance feedback. At the earliest training stages, novices frequently focus on getting faster at the task. This may, as shown here, compromise the evolution of their precision scores, sometimes irreparably, if it is not controlled for as early as possible. Artificial intelligence could help make sure that a trainee reaches her/his optimal individual speed–accuracy trade-off by monitoring individual performance criteria, detecting critical trends at any given moment in time, and alerting the trainee as early as necessary when to slow down and focus on precision, or when to focus on getting faster. It is suggested that, for effective benchmarking, individual training statistics of novices are compared with the statistics of an expert surgeon. The speed–accuracy functions of novices trained in a large number of experimental sessions reveal differences in individual speed–precision strategies, and clarify why such strategies should be automatically detected and controlled for before further training on specific surgical task models, or clinical models, may be envisaged. How expert benchmark statistics may be exploited for automatic performance control is explained.

result.paraphrase: Simulator training for image-guided surgical interventions would benefit from intelligent systems that identify how task performance evolves and manage individual speed–precision strategies by delivering effective automatic performance feedback. In the earliest stages of training, novices often concentrate on becoming faster at the task. As shown here, this can hinder the development of their precision scores, sometimes irreversibly, if it is not addressed as early as possible. Artificial intelligence could help ensure that a trainee attains their optimal personal speed–accuracy trade-off by monitoring individual performance criteria, detecting critical trends at any moment, and alerting the trainee as soon as needed to slow down and prioritize precision, or to speed up. For effective benchmarking, it is suggested that novices’ individual training statistics be compared with those of an expert surgeon. The speed–accuracy functions of novices trained across many experimental sessions reveal differences in individual speed–precision strategies and explain why such strategies should be automatically detected and controlled before further training on specific surgical task models or clinical models is considered. The use of expert benchmark statistics for automatic performance control is also described.
